Return on investment and marginal return

Source: R/contributions.R
roi.Rd

roi() divides each channel's total contribution by its total spend. mroi() asks the different and more useful question of what the next currency unit would return at current spend.

Usage

roi(contributions, spend, by = NULL, index = NULL, periods = NULL)

mroi(spend_level, coefficient, type = "hill", delta = 0.01, ...)

Arguments

contributions

A data frame from contributions(), or a named numeric vector of total contribution per channel.

spend

A data frame of raw (untransformed) spend with one column per channel and one row per period, or a named numeric vector of total spend per channel. Spend columns are read as numbers: a factor is read by its labels, and text that is not a number is an error.

by

Optional group of each row of spend, for one row per channel per group: the name of a column of spend, or a vector (or a data frame of key columns) with one value per row of spend, as given to contributions(). contributions must then come from contributions() with by, and its group column is matched to these groups.

index

Optional period of each row of spend: the name of a column of spend, or a vector with one value per row, as given to contributions(). With index, spend and contributions are matched period by period, within each group when by is supplied, and periods that appear in only one of them are left out, with a message.

periods

Optional vector of the periods to include, compared with the period column of contributions and with index, so that one year or one quarter of a longer decomposition can be reported. When spend is a data frame, periods needs index. When spend gives totals, periods selects contributions only, and the totals must cover the same periods.

spend_level

Current spend level for the channel, in the same units the saturation curve was fitted on: the adstocked level, for a curve applied after adstock as in media_transform().

coefficient

The channel's fitted coefficient.

type

Saturation curve type, as in saturate(), or "none" for a linear response.

delta

Increment used for the numerical derivative, as a fraction of spend_level.

...

Passed to saturate(), for example half_max and shape.

Value

roi() returns a data frame with columns channel, contribution, spend and roi, ordered by descending ROI, with roi set to NA where spend is zero. Channels appearing in only one of the two inputs are omitted, and reported when that happens. With by, a group column comes first and there is one row per channel per group: groups in the order they first appear in contributions, channels by descending ROI within each. Groups found in only one of the two inputs are omitted, with a message. mroi() returns a single number.

Each channel's contribution and spend must cover the same periods. When contributions comes from contributions() and spend is a data frame without index, roi() warns if the number of periods decomposed differs from the number of rows of spend, group by group with by. Give index to match the two period by period instead.

Details

Average ROI and marginal ROI answer different questions and are routinely confused. Average ROI is a scorecard: what did this channel return over the period as a whole. Marginal ROI is the decision variable: what would the next unit return. Only the second one should drive a reallocation, and the two can point in opposite directions.

Where they sit relative to each other depends on the shape of the curve.

For a concave response (saturate_hill() with shape <= 1, Michaelis–Menten, negative exponential, saturate_power()), marginal ROI is below average ROI everywhere, and the gap widens the further up the curve a channel sits. Reallocating on average ROI then systematically over-funds channels that are already saturated, which are exactly the channels that look best on an average-ROI table.

For an S-shaped response (saturate_hill() with shape > 1, the usual way to represent a threshold effect), the curve is convex below its inflection point, and there marginal ROI is above average ROI. A channel in that region has not saturated: each extra pound works harder than the pounds already spent, so a cut there loses more per pound than the average return suggests. Whether the channel should get more budget still depends on how its marginal return compares with other channels' and with break-even.

mroi() differentiates the fitted response curve numerically, so it works for any curve saturate() supports, with a step of delta times spend_level that never falls below a small fraction of the curve's own spend parameter (half_max, km, or the half-life of rate). At spend_level = 0 it is finite and correct wherever the curve's slope at zero is finite: Hill curves with shape >= 1, Michaelis–Menten, exponential and "none". A Hill curve with shape < 1 and a power curve with exponent < 1 rise infinitely steeply at zero, and there mroi() returns the average slope over a short first step, which is large but not a derivative.

Marginal return when the regressor was adstocked

mroi() is the slope of the coefficient times the saturation curve at a single level of the curve's input, the adstocked media. It is a property of the curve, not yet a return on spend, and two things separate the two.

Carryover spreads a unit of spend over many periods. Under a normalised kernel the weights sum to one, so the total extra response to one more unit of spend is roughly the curve's slope, arriving over the kernel's length. Multiplying by the kernel's first weight (1 - decay) gives only the response inside the period of spend; comparing that with an average ROI that counts every period's carryover compares a part with a whole, and understates slow channels several-fold.

And the slope at the mean adstocked level is not the mean of the slope across periods, which matters for flighted media and S-shaped curves.

marginal_roi() handles both by re-running the whole transform on a slightly larger budget. Use it for anything that feeds a budget decision, and use mroi() to read the shape of a curve.

See also

marginal_roi() for marginal return on spend through the full transform, contributions(), response_curve(), spend_for()

Examples

data(mm_weekly)
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")

spec <- lapply(stats::setNames(channels, channels), function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]],
                    shape = truth$shape[[ch]])
))
transformed <- transform_plan(north[channels], spec)

model_data <- transformed
model_data$week <- seq_len(nrow(model_data))
model_data$price <- north$price
model_data$seasonality <- north$seasonality
model_data$holiday <- north$holiday

fit <- stats::lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = model_data)
contrib <- contributions(transformed, fit, index = north$date)

roi(contrib, north[channels])
#>   channel contribution  spend      roi
#> 1  social    132708.89  36716 3.614470
#> 2  search    208306.77  74560 2.793814
#> 3   video    102461.17  53248 1.924226
#> 4 display     40852.88  26937 1.516608
#> 5      tv    349628.86 266978 1.309579

# One row per channel per year: give contributions() and roi() the same `by`
year <- format(north$date, "%Y")
by_year <- contributions(transformed, fit, index = north$date, by = year)
roi(by_year, north[channels], by = year)
#>    group channel contribution spend      roi
#> 1   2023  social     41851.81 11341 3.690310
#> 2   2023  search     69308.42 24754 2.799888
#> 3   2023   video     34499.16 19144 1.802087
#> 4   2023 display     12225.40  8055 1.517741
#> 5   2023      tv    113145.78 93732 1.207120
#> 6   2024  social     48680.52 14037 3.468014
#> 7   2024  search     71022.56 25540 2.780836
#> 8   2024   video     34585.76 17499 1.976442
#> 9   2024 display     14455.69  9626 1.501734
#> 10  2024      tv    112665.80 77978 1.444841
#> 11  2025  social     42176.56 11338 3.719929
#> 12  2025  search     67975.80 24266 2.801277
#> 13  2025   video     33376.25 16605 2.010012
#> 14  2025 display     14171.79  9256 1.531092
#> 15  2025      tv    123817.28 95268 1.299673

# The last year only, with spend matched to contributions week by week
roi(contrib, north[c("date", channels)], index = "date",
    periods = north$date[year == "2025"])
#>   channel contribution spend      roi
#> 1  social     42176.56 11338 3.719929
#> 2  search     67975.80 24266 2.801277
#> 3   video     33376.25 16605 2.010012
#> 4 display     14171.79  9256 1.531092
#> 5      tv    123817.28 95268 1.299673

# Average and marginal return are different questions. marginal_roi()
# re-runs the whole transform on a 1% larger budget, so carryover and
# flighting are both accounted for; its `roi` column matches
# roi(contrib, north[channels]). Display's average pound returns about 1.5,
# but its next pound returns less than it costs.
marginal_roi(north, stats::coef(fit), spec = spec)
#>   channel  spend contribution      roi      mroi
#> 1      tv 266978    349628.86 1.309579 1.2534121
#> 2   video  53248    102461.17 1.924226 1.1960500
#> 3  search  74560    208306.77 2.793814 1.3489844
#> 4  social  36716    132708.89 3.614470 2.0891914
#> 5 display  26937     40852.88 1.516608 0.9324061
